title: Strings: Basics & Syntax
tagline: String creation, quotes, immutability, concatenation, repetition, and membership

items.title: String Creation & Quotes
items.explain: Strings are sequences of characters enclosed in single, double, or triple quotes (for multi-line strings).
items.code:
s1 = 'hello'
s2 = "world"
s3 = '''line 1
line 2'''
print(s1, s2)
print(s3)

items.title: String Immutability
items.explain: Strings in Python are immutable; characters cannot be reassigned or modified directly after creation.
items.output: TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment

items.title: Concatenation (+)
items.explain: Combines multiple strings into a new string using the + operator.
items.code:
a = "hello"
b = " world"
result = a + b
print(result)

items.title: Repetition (*)
items.explain: Repeats a string a specified number of times using the * operator.

items.title: Membership Operators (in, not in)
items.explain: Checks whether a specific substring exists inside another string.
items.syntax: sub in string | sub not in string
items.code:
print("ell" in "hello")
print("xyz" not in "hello")
print("z" in "hello")

items.title: String Comparison
items.explain: Compares strings character-by-character based on their Unicode (ASCII) values lexicographically.
items.syntax: str1 == str2 | str1 < str2 | str1 > str2

items.title: String Iteration
items.explain: Iterates through characters one-by-one in a string using a for loop or converts to list.

title: Strings: Indexing & Slicing
tagline: Accessing characters by index, negative indices, and slicing intervals

items.title: Positive Indexing
items.explain: Gets a character from a string using its zero-based position.

items.title: Negative Indexing
items.explain: Gets characters counting backwards from the end of the string, where -1 is the last character.

items.title: Basic Slicing [start:stop]
items.explain: Extracts a portion of a string from start index up to but not including stop index.
items.code:
s = "hello world"
print(s[0:5])
print(s[6:11])
print(s[:5])
print(s[6:])

items.title: Step Slicing [start:stop:step]
items.explain: Extracts characters jumping by a specified step stride.

items.title: Reversing a String [::-1]
items.explain: Reverses an entire string cleanly using a negative step in slice notation.

items.title: Slicing with Negative Indices
items.explain: Extracts substrings using relative negative start and stop offsets from the end.

title: Strings: Case Conversion
tagline: Converting letters between uppercase, lowercase, titlecase, and capitalized styles

items.title: upper()
items.explain: Converts all lowercase letters in the string to uppercase.

items.title: lower()
items.explain: Converts all uppercase letters in the string to lowercase.

items.title: title()
items.explain: Capitalizes the first letter of each word in the string.

items.title: capitalize()
items.explain: Capitalizes only the very first character of the string, making all others lowercase.

items.title: swapcase()
items.explain: Inverts letter casing: converts uppercase letters to lowercase and lowercase to uppercase.

items.title: casefold()
items.explain: Performs aggressive, Unicode-aware lowercase conversion, ideal for caseless comparisons.
items.code:
print("HELLO".casefold())
print("ß".casefold())  # German sharp s expands to ss

title: Strings: Searching & Finding
tagline: Locating substrings, checking prefixes and suffixes, counting occurrences

items.title: find()
items.explain: Returns the first index of a substring, or -1 if the substring is not present.

items.title: rfind()
items.explain: Returns the last (highest) index of a substring, or -1 if absent.

items.title: index()
items.explain: Returns the first index of a substring, but raises ValueError if not found.

items.title: rindex()
items.explain: Returns the last index of a substring; raises ValueError if not found.

items.title: count()
items.explain: Counts the total number of non-overlapping occurrences of a substring.

items.title: startswith()
items.explain: Checks whether the string starts with a specified prefix or tuple of prefixes.

items.title: endswith()
items.explain: Checks whether the string ends with a specified suffix or tuple of suffixes.

title: Strings: Content Checking
tagline: Methods checking alphabetic, digit, whitespace, identifier, and formatting properties

items.title: isalpha()
items.explain: Checks whether every character in the string is an alphabetic letter (a-z, A-Z).

items.title: isalnum()
items.explain: Checks whether every character in the string is alphanumeric (letters or numbers).

items.title: isdigit()
items.explain: Checks whether every character in the string is a digit (0-9).

items.title: isnumeric()
items.explain: Checks whether characters represent numeric values, including fractions and superscript digits.

items.title: isdecimal()
items.explain: Checks whether all characters are strict base-10 decimal digits.

items.title: isspace()
items.explain: Checks whether every character in the string is whitespace (spaces, tabs, newlines).

items.title: islower()
items.explain: Checks whether the string contains at least one cased character and all cased characters are lowercase.

items.title: isupper()
items.explain: Checks whether the string contains at least one cased character and all cased characters are uppercase.

items.title: istitle()
items.explain: Checks whether the string follows title-casing (first character of words uppercase, rest lowercase).

items.title: isascii()
items.explain: Checks whether all characters in the string are ASCII characters (U+0000 to U+007F).

items.title: isidentifier()
items.explain: Checks whether the string is a syntactically valid Python identifier or variable name.

items.title: isprintable()
items.explain: Checks whether all characters in the string can be printed (returns False for control characters like \n).

title: Strings: Splitting & Joining
tagline: Tokenizing strings into lists and recombining iterables into formatted strings

items.title: split()
items.explain: Splits a string into a list using a specified delimiter (defaults to whitespace).
items.code:
s = "apple,banana,cherry"
print(s.split(","))

words = "one two   three"
print(words.split())

items.title: rsplit()
items.explain: Splits a string starting from the right side up to maxsplit times.

items.title: splitlines()
items.explain: Splits a multi-line string at newline boundaries into a list of lines.

items.title: join()
items.explain: Concatenates elements of an iterable into a single string using the caller string as delimiter.

items.title: partition()
items.explain: Splits the string into a 3-tuple: (before, separator, after) at the first occurrence of separator.

items.title: rpartition()
items.explain: Splits the string into a 3-tuple at the last occurrence of separator.

title: Strings: Removing & Replacing
tagline: Trimming whitespace, stripping prefixes and suffixes, replacing substrings

items.title: strip()
items.explain: Removes leading and trailing whitespace or specified characters from both ends.

items.title: lstrip()
items.explain: Removes leading whitespace or specified characters from the left side.

items.title: rstrip()
items.explain: Removes trailing whitespace or specified characters from the right side.

items.title: removeprefix()
items.explain: Removes the exact prefix string if the string begins with it (Python 3.9+).

items.title: removesuffix()
items.explain: Removes the exact suffix string if the string ends with it (Python 3.9+).

items.title: replace()
items.explain: Replaces occurrences of an old substring with a new substring up to count times.

title: Strings: Alignment & Padding
tagline: Centering, left/right aligning, and zero-padding numbers or text

items.title: center()
items.explain: Centers the string within a field of specified width, padded with spaces or fillchar.

items.title: ljust()
items.explain: Left-aligns the string and pads the right side to reach total width.

items.title: rjust()
items.explain: Right-aligns the string and pads the left side to reach total width.

items.title: zfill()
items.explain: Pads the left side of a numeric string with zeros to reach width, handling +/- signs properly.

title: Strings: Formatting & f-Strings
tagline: Modern f-strings, str.format(), format_map, and format specifiers

items.title: f-Strings (Modern String Formatting)
items.explain: Prefix string with f to embed expressions, variables, and specifiers directly inside {}.
items.code:
name = "Sajin"
age = 20
score = 94.567
print(f"{name} is {age} years old")
print(f"Score: {score:.1f}")

items.title: format()
items.explain: Inserts positional and keyword arguments into {} placeholders.

items.title: format_map()
items.explain: Formats using key-value pairs taken directly from a dictionary or mapping.

title: Strings: Encoding & Translation
tagline: Byte encoding and character-level transliteration tables

items.title: encode()
items.explain: Encodes string into bytes using a specified encoding (UTF-8 by default).

items.title: str.maketrans()
items.explain: Creates a one-to-one character mapping table for use with translate().

items.title: translate()
items.explain: Replaces and removes characters according to a translation table created with maketrans().

title: Strings: Built-in Functions
tagline: General Python built-ins essential when working with strings (len, ord, chr, etc.)

items.title: len()
items.explain: Returns the total number of characters in the string.

items.title: str()
items.explain: Converts any object into its string representation.

items.title: ord()
items.explain: Returns the integer Unicode / ASCII code point of a single character.

items.title: chr()
items.explain: Converts an integer Unicode code point into its corresponding character.

items.title: ascii()
items.explain: Returns an ASCII-only string representation, escaping non-ASCII characters with \x, \u, or \U.

items.title: repr()
items.explain: Returns the official, printable string representation of an object (including surrounding quotes).

title: Strings: string Module & Templates
tagline: Standard string constants, capwords, and $-based string.Template

items.title: string Module Constants
items.explain: Predefined character sets for letters, digits, punctuation, and whitespace.

items.title: string.capwords()
items.explain: Splits words by separator, capitalizes each word, and joins them back together.

items.title: string.Template ($ substitution)
items.explain: Safe, simple $-based string substitution designed for user-provided templates without code execution risks.
items.syntax:
from string import Template
t = Template('Hello $name')
t.substitute(name='...')
items.code:
from string import Template
t = Template("Hello $name, your score is $score")
result = t.substitute(name="Sajin", score=98)
print(result)

items.title: Template.safe_substitute()
items.explain: Substitutes placeholders, but leaves missing placeholders untouched instead of raising KeyError.
items.code:
from string import Template
t = Template("Hello $name, age $age")
# Missing 'age' does not raise KeyError:
print(t.safe_substitute(name="Sajin"))

items.title: Template.get_identifiers() & is_valid()
items.explain: Inspects placeholder names and validates whether a template string has well-formed syntax (Python 3.11+).
items.code:
from string import Template
t = Template("User: $user, Role: $role")
print(t.get_identifiers())
print(t.is_valid())

title: Lists: Basics & Creation
tagline: List creation, heterogeneous data types, mutability, and differences from tuples

items.title: Creating Lists
items.explain: Lists are ordered, mutable collections enclosed in square brackets [] or created via list() constructor.
items.code:
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = list("cat")
c = list(range(4))
print(a)
print(b)
print(c)

items.title: Empty Lists
items.explain: Creates an empty list with [] or list() for accumulating elements later.
items.code:
a = []
b = list()
print(a, len(a))
print(type(b))

items.title: Mixed Data Types & Nested Lists
items.explain: A list can contain elements of differing types including ints, floats, strings, booleans, and other lists.

items.title: List Mutability
items.explain: Lists are mutable: their elements can be modified, appended, or deleted in place without creating a new list.

items.title: Lists vs. Tuples
items.explain: Lists are mutable [ ] with dynamic sizing. Tuples are immutable ( ) with fixed length and hashability.
items.code:
my_list = [1, 2]
my_tuple = (1, 2)
my_list.append(3)
print("List:", my_list)
# my_tuple cannot be modified in place

title: Lists: Indexing & Access
tagline: Positive, negative, and nested indices, modifying elements in place, index errors

items.title: Positive Indexing
items.explain: Accesses elements starting at index 0 up to len(a) - 1.

items.title: Negative Indexing
items.explain: Accesses elements from the right end, where -1 is the last item.

items.title: Indexing Nested Lists
items.explain: Chains brackets to reach inside inner lists: outer[row][col].

items.title: IndexError Caveat
items.explain: Attempting to read or write an index beyond the current list boundary raises IndexError.
items.output: Caught: list index out of range

items.title: Modifying Elements In Place
items.explain: Assigns a new value to an existing position in the list.

title: Lists: Slicing Operations
tagline: Sublist extraction, strides, step reversals, and slice assignments

items.title: Basic Slicing [start:stop]
items.explain: Extracts a new sublist from start up to stop (exclusive).

items.title: Shallow Copy via Slice [:]
items.explain: Omitting both start and stop creates a shallow clone of the list.
items.code:
orig = [1, 2, 3]
copy_list = orig[:]
copy_list.append(4)
print("Orig:", orig)
print("Copy:", copy_list)

items.title: Slice with Step [::step]
items.explain: Takes elements in increments of step.

items.title: Reversing a List via Slicing [::-1]
items.explain: Returns a new reversed list without mutating the original list.

items.title: Modifying Multiple Elements via Slicing
items.explain: Replaces a slice with elements from an iterable, even if the length differs.

title: Lists: Core Methods
tagline: The 11 essential list methods: append, extend, insert, pop, remove, sort, etc.

items.title: append()
items.explain: Adds an element to the very end of the list in O(1) amortized time.

items.title: extend()
items.explain: Unpacks and appends all elements from another iterable to the end of the list.

items.title: insert()
items.explain: Inserts an item before a specified index position, shifting succeeding elements right.

items.title: remove()
items.explain: Removes the first occurrence of a value from the list; raises ValueError if not found.

items.title: pop()
items.explain: Removes and returns the item at index (defaults to last item index -1).
items.code:
stack = [10, 20, 30]
top = stack.pop()
first = stack.pop(0)
print("popped:", top, first)
print("remaining:", stack)

items.title: clear()
items.explain: Removes all elements from the list, making it empty [].

items.title: index()
items.explain: Returns the zero-based index of the first occurrence of a value.

items.title: count()
items.explain: Returns the total number of occurrences of a value in the list.

items.title: reverse()
items.explain: Reverses the elements of the list in-place (mutates original list, returns None).

items.title: copy()
items.explain: Returns a shallow copy of the list.
items.code:
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a.copy()
b.append(99)
print("a:", a)
print("b:", b)

title: Lists: Shallow vs. Deep Copy
tagline: Understanding object references, shallow copying, copy.deepcopy, and reference traps

items.title: Shallow Copy (list.copy)
items.explain: Creates a new outer list container, but inner nested objects are still shared references.
items.code:
a = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
b = a.copy()
b[0].append(99)
print("a:", a)
print("b:", b)

items.title: Deep Copy (copy.deepcopy)
items.explain: Recursively clones the outer list and every nested list/object inside it independently.
items.code:
import copy
a = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
b = copy.deepcopy(a)
b[0].append(99)
print("a:", a)
print("b:", b)

items.title: Assignment (b = a) vs. Copy
items.explain: b = a does NOT copy; it merely creates another variable name pointing to the exact same list in memory.
items.syntax: b = a  # Same list in memory!
items.code:
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a
b.append(4)
print("a:", a)
print("a is b:", a is b)

items.title: == vs. is Operator
items.explain: == tests whether two lists contain equal values; is tests whether both variables refer to the exact same object in RAM.
items.code:
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = [1, 2, 3]
print("a == b:", a == b)
print("a is b:", a is b)
items.output:
a == b: True
a is b: False

title: Lists: Sorting & Custom Keys
tagline: list.sort() in place vs sorted(), reverse=True, key functions, lambda, and tuple sorting

items.title: list.sort() (In-place)
items.explain: Sorts the list in place and returns None. Mutates the original list.
items.code:
nums = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9]
res = nums.sort()
print("nums:", nums)
print("returns:", res)

items.title: sorted() (New List)
items.explain: Built-in function that takes any iterable and returns a new sorted list, leaving original intact.
items.code:
nums = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5]
res = sorted(nums)
print("res:", res)
print("orig:", nums)

items.title: Descending Order (reverse=True)
items.explain: Passes reverse=True to sort in descending order.

items.title: Sorting by Length (key=len)
items.explain: Applies the len function to every element before comparing.

items.title: Sorting with lambda
items.explain: Uses an anonymous function as the key extractor for custom comparisons.

items.title: Multiple Sorting Criteria
items.explain: Returns a tuple from the key function to sort by primary then secondary attributes.

title: Lists: Built-in Functions & Loops
tagline: len, sum, min, max, any, all, enumerate, in, and unpacking

items.title: len(), sum(), min(), max()
items.explain: Statistical and length operations supported natively on numeric lists.
items.code:
nums = [10, 20, 5, 30]
print("len:", len(nums))
print("sum:", sum(nums))
print("min:", min(nums))
print("max:", max(nums))

items.title: any() and all()
items.explain: any() returns True if at least one element is truthy. all() returns True if all elements are truthy.

items.title: enumerate()
items.explain: Yields pairs of (index, item) when looping over a list, eliminating manual counter variables.
items.syntax: for i, item in enumerate(iterable, start=0):

items.title: List Unpacking & Extended Unpacking
items.explain: Unpacks elements into individual variables, using * to collect surplus items into a sublist.
items.code:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
a, *b, c = nums
print("a:", a)
print("b:", b)
print("c:", c)

title: Lists: 2D & Nested Lists (Matrices)
tagline: Matrix row/col traversal, flattening, transposition, and avoiding the multiplication trap

items.title: The 2D List Repetition Trap ([[]]*n)
items.explain: Using [[0]*3]*3 duplicates the same inner list 3 times; modifying one row affects every row!

items.title: Correct 2D List Creation
items.explain: Use a list comprehension to create distinct inner lists for each row.
items.syntax: matrix = [[0 for _ in range(cols)] for _ in range(rows)]
items.code:
matrix = [[0] * 3 for _ in range(3)]
matrix[0][0] = 99
print(matrix)

items.title: Traversing a 2D Matrix
items.explain: Iterates over matrix rows and columns with nested loops or enumerate.
items.syntax:
for r in range(rows):
    for c in range(cols):

items.title: Flattening a 2D List
items.explain: Flattens rows into a single 1D list using comprehension.
items.syntax: flattened = [item for row in matrix for item in row]
items.code:
matrix = [[1, 2], [3, 4], [5, 6]]
flat = [x for row in matrix for x in row]
print(flat)

items.title: Transposing a Matrix
items.explain: Swaps rows and columns using zip(*matrix) or nested comprehensions.
items.code:
matrix = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]
transposed = [list(col) for col in zip(*matrix)]
print(transposed)

title: Lists: List Comprehensions
tagline: Elegant syntax for mapping, filtering, transforming, and constructing new lists

items.title: Basic List Comprehension
items.explain: Constructs a new list by applying an expression to each item in an iterable.
items.code:
squares = [x**2 for x in range(5)]
print(squares)

items.title: Filtering with if
items.explain: Includes only items matching the conditional predicate at the end.
items.syntax: [expr for item in iterable if condition]
items.code:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]
evens = [x for x in nums if x % 2 == 0]
print(evens)

items.title: Conditional Expression (if-else)
items.explain: Places ternary expression (val_if if cond else val_else) before the for clause.
items.syntax: [val_if if cond else val_else for item in iterable]
items.code:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
labels = ["even" if x % 2 == 0 else "odd" for x in nums]
print(labels)

items.title: Multiple for Clauses in Comprehensions
items.explain: Loops through multiple sequences in order of outer to inner loop.
items.syntax: [(x, y) for x in listA for y in listB]
items.code:
pairs = [(x, y) for x in [1, 2] for y in ['a', 'b']]
print(pairs)

items.title: Common Useful Patterns
items.explain: Filters out empty strings or None values and cleans input sequences cleanly.
items.syntax: cleaned = [x for x in items if x is not None and x != '']
items.code:
raw = ["apple", "", "banana", None, "cherry"]
clean = [s.upper() for s in raw if s]
print(clean)

title: Tuples: Basics & Creation
tagline: Tuple syntax, empty tuples, single-element comma rule, and creation without parentheses

items.title: Normal Tuple Creation
items.explain: Tuples are immutable ordered collections written with parentheses (1, 2, 3) or tuple() constructor.

items.title: Empty Tuple ()
items.explain: An empty tuple is constructed with () or tuple().

items.title: Single-Element Tuple with Comma (x,) ⭐
items.explain: A trailing comma is REQUIRED to make a single-element tuple. Without the comma, (10) is merely an integer.
items.syntax: single = (10,)  # comma makes it a tuple!
items.code:
a = (10,)
b = (10)
print("a:", type(a))
print("b:", type(b))

items.title: Tuples Without Parentheses
items.explain: In Python, the comma creates the tuple, meaning parentheses are optional in many contexts.

items.title: Mixed Data Types in Tuples
items.explain: Tuples can hold elements of any data type, including strings, numbers, booleans, and lists.
items.code:
person = ("Sajin", 19, 62.5, True)
print(person)
for item in person:
    print(type(item))

title: Tuples: Indexing & Slicing
tagline: Accessing tuple elements, negative offsets, and slicing variations

items.title: Positive Indexing
items.explain: Accesses elements starting from index 0 up to len(t) - 1.

items.title: Negative Indexing
items.explain: Counts backwards from the end of the tuple.

items.title: Tuple Slicing [start:stop]
items.explain: Extracts a new tuple from start up to stop (stop is NOT included).

items.title: Slicing with Step [start:stop:step]
items.explain: Extracts elements with a stride or negative step to reverse.

title: Tuples: Immutability & Safety
tagline: Why tuples cannot be changed, and how nested mutable objects behave

items.title: Tuples are Immutable
items.explain: Once created, elements cannot be reassigned, added, or deleted; attempting to do so raises TypeError.
items.output: TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment

items.title: Modifying Mutable Objects Inside Tuples
items.explain: A tuple's references are fixed, but if a tuple holds a mutable object (like a list), that inner list can still be modified.

items.title: Rebinding Variable vs. Mutating
items.explain: Assigning t = t + (4,) does not mutate the old tuple; it allocates a brand-new tuple and rebinds t.
items.code:
t = (1, 2, 3)
old_id = id(t)
t = t + (4,)
print("New tuple:", t)
print("Same object in RAM?:", id(t) == old_id)
items.output:
New tuple: (1, 2, 3, 4)
Same object in RAM?: False

title: Tuples: Packing & Unpacking
tagline: Tuple packing, variable assignment unpacking, extended * unpacking, and swapping

items.title: Tuple Packing
items.explain: Multiple comma-separated values are automatically packed into a single tuple object.

items.title: Tuple Unpacking
items.explain: Extracts elements of a tuple into distinct variables simultaneously (must match element count).
items.code:
point = (4, 9)
x, y = point
print(f"x={x}, y={y}")

items.title: Extended Unpacking (*)
items.explain: Uses an asterisk (*) on one variable to capture leftover elements as a list.
items.code:
t = (1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
a, *b, c = t
print("a:", a)
print("b:", b, type(b))
print("c:", c)

items.title: Variable Swapping (a, b = b, a)
items.explain: Swaps two variables cleanly without requiring any temporary third variable, utilizing tuple packing/unpacking.
items.code:
a = 5
b = 10
a, b = b, a
print(f"a={a}, b={b}")

items.title: Unpacking in Loops
items.explain: Unpacks tuple pairs directly in the for loop header.

title: Tuples: Methods & Built-ins
tagline: The only two native tuple methods: count() and index(), plus len, sorted, min, max, sum

items.title: count()
items.explain: Returns the total number of times a specified value appears in the tuple.

items.title: index()
items.explain: Returns the first zero-based index where value is found; raises ValueError if not present.

items.title: len() with Tuples
items.explain: Returns the total count of items stored in the tuple.

items.title: sorted() with Tuples
items.explain: Returns a new sorted LIST from the tuple. Use tuple(sorted(t)) if a tuple is desired.
items.code:
t = (3, 1, 4, 2)
res_list = sorted(t)
res_tup = tuple(sorted(t))
print("list:", res_list)
print("tuple:", res_tup)

items.title: min(), max(), sum() with Tuples
items.explain: Built-in aggregation functions operate directly across numeric tuples.
items.code:
t = (10, 40, 20, 30)
print("min:", min(t))
print("max:", max(t))
print("sum:", sum(t))

title: Tuples: Operations & Comparison
tagline: Concatenation, repetition, membership testing, and lexicographical comparisons

items.title: Tuple Concatenation (+)
items.explain: Joins two tuples together into a brand-new tuple without modifying either original.
items.code:
a = (1, 2)
b = (3, 4)
c = a + b
print(c)

items.title: Tuple Repetition (*)
items.explain: Repeats a tuple's elements n times into a new tuple.

items.title: Membership Operators (in, not in)
items.explain: Checks whether a value is present in the tuple.
items.syntax: value in tuple | value not in tuple
items.code:
t = (10, 20, 30)
print(20 in t)
print(99 not in t)

items.title: Comparing Tuples
items.explain: Tuples are compared element-by-element from left to right. If equal, the shorter tuple is smaller.

title: Tuples: Conversions & Advanced Patterns
tagline: Converting to/from lists, dict keys, hashing, function returns, and zip()

items.title: Converting Iterables to Tuples
items.explain: Converts lists, strings, sets, or ranges into tuples using tuple().

items.title: Tuple → List → Tuple Pattern
items.explain: When a tuple must be altered, convert to a list, mutate it, and convert back to a tuple.
items.code:
t = (1, 2, 3)
lst = list(t)
lst.append(4)
t = tuple(lst)
print(t)

items.title: Multiple Function Returns
items.explain: A Python function returning multiple comma-separated values returns a single tuple.

items.title: Tuples as Dictionary Keys & Hashing
items.explain: Because tuples are immutable, they are hashable and can be dictionary keys (provided they contain only hashable elements).
items.code:
coords = {}
coords[(0, 0)] = "Origin"
coords[(3, 4)] = "Point A"
print(coords[(0, 0)])
print(hash((1, 2)))

items.title: zip() Producing Tuples
items.explain: The built-in zip() combines elements from multiple iterables into tuples of grouped pairs.
items.code:
names = ["Alice", "Bob", "Charlie"]
scores = [85, 92, 78]
combined = list(zip(names, scores))
print(combined)
